title: Surprise! Scientists Find a Brand-New Penguin Species
summary:
Imagine a penguin hiding in plain sight for more than 100 years. That's exactly what happened on the Kerguelen Islands — nicknamed the Desolation Islands — nearly 2,000 miles from any place where people live. Scientists just announced that a group of gentoo penguins living there is actually a brand-new species. It's the first new penguin species named in more than 100 years!

Gentoo penguins have black backs and white bellies. They look a lot like other gentoos. But their DNA is clearly different. Scientists call this a "cryptic species" — an animal that looks like its cousins but is really its own kind.

The new penguin is called Pygoscelis kerguelensis. The study also found that three other gentoo groups are different enough to be their own species too. One of them, the southern gentoo, is the only one that lives in Antarctica.

Why does this matter? Because two of these new species could be in trouble as the planet warms. "The gentoo is of most concern in the sub-Antarctic region," said scientist Juliana Vianna. Now that we know these penguins are separate species, we can work to protect them.
why_it_matters: It shows that even today scientists can discover a brand-new animal hiding in plain sight — and that learning a creature is its own species is the first step to keeping it safe for the future.

background_read: The Kerguelen Islands (a group of cold, windy islands in the southern Indian Ocean) have no towns or farms — mostly scientists visit them.
DNA (the set of instructions inside every living thing) lets scientists compare animals that look almost the same and discover they are actually different.
Penguins are birds that cannot fly but are amazing swimmers; gentoo penguins are one of the most common kinds in the cold southern oceans.

perspectives.description: Finding a new species after 100 years is thrilling — it proves there is still so much about nature we haven't discovered yet.
They point out that two of the new species could struggle as the planet warms, so the discovery comes with a warning.
They say we needed DNA tests, not just looking at the birds, to be sure these penguins are really different kinds.
